extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematics educators, and students considering submitting to MAA periodicals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and submitting articles, notes, problems, and blog posts to the various MAA periodicals (American Mathematical Monthly, CMJ, Mathematics Magazine, Math Horizons, FOCUS, Convergence, Math Values). Covers audience, formats, length limits, review process, and practical submission advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: American Mathematical Monthly — appropriate audience and article types
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts appropriate for a broad audience of professional mathematicians presented in an engaging manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main submission types: articles (more than five pages), notes (under five pages), filler (very focused articles of less than a page), problem proposals and solutions, and book reviews. If you have questions or submissions, contact the Monthly editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: College Mathematics Journal (CMJ) — focus and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses mainly on mathematics encountered during the first two years of college; targets faculty at two-year and similar institutions and their students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishes well-written articles (under twelve pages), classroom capsules (under three pages), problems and solutions, book reviews, and media highlights. Contact the CMJ editor for submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics Magazine — audience and topical scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishes content appealing to a broad mathematical audience including strong undergraduate students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions may focus on mathematics or math education, math and the humanities, the history of math, mathematics and art, or related fields. Read recent issues to gauge style and level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math Horizons — undergraduate focus and word/image expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets enthusiastic undergraduate-level readers with self-contained articles that promote reader engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best submissions have a maximum of 2200 words and should include colorful images. The magazine includes interviews, puzzles, book reviews, and career opportunities; contact the editor for queries.

rubrics_metrics.name: MAA FOCUS — length and topical emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The MAA's news magazine for members; accepts short articles and column submissions on pedagogy, outreach, and community issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can submit articles up to 1600 words or one of eight columns up to 1200 words. FOCUS also accepts puzzles, cover art, member profile suggestions, and more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence — history of mathematics & K-12–16 teaching use
rubrics_metrics.description: A refereed, open-access online journal on the history of mathematics and its use in teaching subjects typical for grades 8–16.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions can include historically based classroom activities, translations of primary sources, expository history articles tied to the grades 8–16 curriculum, or classroom images. Contact the Convergence editors for submission details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math Values blog — format and values-guided content
rubrics_metrics.description: Blog site exploring diverse voices in mathematics guided by values of Inclusivity, Community, Teaching & Learning, and Communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions can include thought-provoking essays, inspiring teaching tidbits, stories of people/communities in mathematics, or ideas for making mathematics more inclusive. Blogs are generally about 1000 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read recent issues to understand audience and style
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to gain familiarity with a particular periodical is to read several recent issues of that publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps you understand the audience, the style of the publication, and the level of mathematics. MAA members and many libraries provide access; some venues (Convergence, Math Values) are freely available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve as a referee to learn reviewing and improve writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Offering to referee is a way to learn about a journal before you submit and to improve your expository skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If invited to referee, you'll receive guidelines for reviewing that help you evaluate others' papers and guide your own future submissions. Refereeing experience enhances writing skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the prospective readers in mind; make novelty accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing, remember you are probably writing about ideas your audience has not seen before; novelty must be presented so readers can engage with it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with the audience's background in mind; clarity and accessible exposition are essential. After writing, get colleagues' feedback on clarity, style, and grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow submission guidelines and remove identifying information when required
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you determine the most appropriate periodical, read and follow that periodical's submission guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Monthly, CMJ, and Mathematics Magazine use a double-blind review process — remove all identifying information before submission. Read the MAA submission page for detailed instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect typical review timelines and variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the review timelines vary by periodical and review type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind reviewed journals (Monthly, CMJ, Math Magazine) typically take three to six months, though this can be longer or shorter depending on referees' schedules and external factors. Other periodicals (Math Horizons, FOCUS, Convergence, Math Values) often provide decisions within a few weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret editorial decisions constructively (reject / revise / accept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions commonly fall into reject, revise, or accept; each should be handled professionally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rejected, set it aside then read feedback later to use comments as guideposts for improvement or to find a better fit. If asked to revise, make adjustments or rewrite parts per reviewers' recommendations. If accepted, follow final instructions from the editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use submission as part of professional development
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting and responding to reviews is a growth process that improves mathematics communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage your strengths, choose an appropriate periodical, and use feedback from the review process to improve future writing. Encouragement: 'Publication Begins with Submission.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and content expectations per periodical
rubrics_metrics.description: Each MAA periodical has specific expectations about length, audience level, and content type that determine fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Monthly (engaging exposition for professionals), CMJ (first-two-years college level, <12 pages), Math Horizons (undergraduate-engaging, ≤2200 words, colorful images), FOCUS (news/features ≤1600 words or columns ≤1200), Math Values (~1000-word blogs). Check the specific editor/contact for details.
